newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dollar in slow motion rally.
newsitem.headline: Australian dollar in slow motion rally.

text.p: The Australian dollar continued its slow motion rally Tuesday as it added a few more ticks on the day but again failed to clear key resistance.
The currency took a look at the US$0.7535 barrier offshore as a couple of U.S. and European banks bought in a thin market, but lapsed on a lack of follow-through demand.

Selling of AUD/yen out of Tokyo encouraged the market's natural caution after a month of steady dollar decline, although dealers reckoned the currency was overdue a good bounce given it had lost around three cents in that time. Stops were thought to be building around US$0.7540 which could see it to US$0.7580.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local currency was poised at US$0.7518/23 having eased from an early US$0.7530/35, but was still ahead of Monday's late US$0.7510/15.
Support was seen at 75 cents and more importantly around last week's floor at US$0.7470, while pivotal resistance was put at SU$0.7630 and US$0.7680.

On the crosses it ended easier on the yen at 85.95/05 yen from 86.63/78 late Monday, but above it slows after faithfully tracking a choppy US$/yen. The initial weakness was caused by comments from Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto urging the U.S. to cooperate on stabilizing exchange rates.
If the dollar were too weak, Hashimoto said, Japan might be tempted to sell its holdings of Treasuries and buy gold.
Treasury prices slid in response and Wall Street dived 2.47 percent as investors took profits.

But Hashimoto later moved to repair the damage issuing a statement through the MOF that his remarks were misinterpreted and Japan had never sold Treasuries in the past because of the over-riding importance of the U.S.-Japan relationship.
This helped the U.S. dollar bounce to 114.44/50 from a 114.00 trough but still left it short of Monday's 115.20.
In trade weighted terms the A$ ended at 57.1 from 57.2.
A lack of domestic data had the market looking elsewhere for inspiration and some hoped to find it in the Bank of Japan's Tankan survey of business sentiment on Wednesday.

This is regarded as a bellweather of both the economy and interest rates, so much so that it is almost an axiom amongst analysts that the BOJ would not tighten monetary policy unless the main diffusion index was positive two quarters in a row.

This index measures the sentiment of large manufacturing firms and showed a reading of plus 2.0 in the March quarter, the first positive result since November 1991. Another positive number, therefore, could well be taken as an omen of a hike.
Some analysts have been nudging down their forecasts for the index recently, however, as the aftershock of a VAT hike in April cast a cloud over business sentiment.
Indeed, market rumours abounded today it would be quite a bit softer than previously thought. Median estimates are for a reading of minus 0.8 but range from minus four to plus four.

A weak result would tend to support the A$ since it would imply there was less risk of the BOJ raising rates in the next few months if not the rest of the year. Analysts did have a caveat, however, in that the reliability of the data would be in question due to the economic volatility caused by the VAT rise.

Incidentally, the main diffusion index has a good historical correlation with the Reserve Bank's commodity price index reflecting Japan's position as the largest single consumer of Australian commodities.
A sustained recovery in the index therefore, should be positive for the A$ over time even if it meant Japanese interest rates might also be nudged higher.

The Tankan survey also includes important readings in the real economy such as manufacturer's plans for capital investment and employment intentions, which may be more useful than the main index itself. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
